title: Review: Wave phenomena; Standing waves and resonance; Doppler effect
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: C.5#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; C.5.4#xt2 term and clue written for the game; C.5.2#xt1 term and clue written for the game; C.4#c17 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Doppler effect
items.clue: The change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other.

items.label: Blueshift
items.clue: Displacement of spectral lines to shorter wavelengths, showing that a star is approaching.

items.label: Wavefront
items.clue: A surface joining points of equal phase; these are crowded together ahead of a moving source.

items.label: Damping
items.clue: The removal of energy from an oscillating system by resistive forces (such as friction or air resistance), which transfer the energy to the internal energy of the system and its surroundings.

questions.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment, monochromatic red light is incident normally on the slits and the fringe separation on the screen is 2.0 mm. Which single change would make the fringe separation 4.0 mm?

options.text: Doubling the distance between the centres of the slits
Using blue light, of shorter wavelength, in place of the red
Halving the width of each slit, keeping their separation
Halving the distance between the centres of the two slits

questions.explanation: s = λD/d, so s is inversely proportional to d: halving the slit separation doubles s from 2.0 mm to 4.0 mm.

questions.stem: A string of length 0.80 m is fixed at both ends. The speed of waves on the string is 240 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of the third harmonic?

options.text: 450 Hz
900 Hz
300 Hz
150 Hz

questions.explanation: With a node at each fixed end, the third harmonic has three loops, each λ/2 long: λ₃ = 2L/3 = 2 × 0.80/3 = 0.533 m. f₃ = v/λ₃ = 240/0.533 = 450 Hz (equivalently 3 × 150 Hz).

questions.stem: A singer shatters a wine glass by singing one steady note close to it. Which condition is essential for this to happen?

options.text: The note is very loud, whatever frequency the singer chooses.
The note is the highest frequency that the singer is able to produce.
The note's frequency is equal to a natural frequency of the glass.
The sound echoes inside the bowl of the glass and builds up.

questions.explanation: This is resonance. At a natural frequency of the glass, the sound pushes the glass in step with its own vibration, so energy builds up cycle after cycle until the amplitude is large enough to break the glass.

questions.stem: In a Doppler ultrasound scan, a probe on the skin emits ultrasound of frequency f into an artery. The blood in the artery flows towards the probe. The probe detects the ultrasound reflected back from the moving blood cells. How does the frequency of the detected ultrasound compare with f?

options.text: Higher than f, and higher still when the blood flows faster
Equal to f, as reflection leaves a wave's frequency unchanged
Lower than f, as the ultrasound loses energy on reflection
Higher than f, by more if the artery is nearer the probe

questions.stem: A wavefront diagram shows the sound from a stationary source in still air as circular wavefronts centred on the source. An observer walks directly towards the source at constant speed. Which statement about the waves and the observer is correct?

options.text: The wavelength is unchanged, but the observer meets the wavefronts more often.
The observer's motion squeezes the wavefronts, so the wavelength is shorter.
The observer detects the emitted frequency, as the source sets it.
The frequency detected rises steadily as the observer nears the source.

questions.stem: A source moving directly away from an observer emits light of frequency 5.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The observer detects the light with a wavelength 0.20% greater than the wavelength emitted. What frequency does the observer detect?
questions.explanation: Δλ/λ = 0.20% = 0.0020. Since c = fλ is the same for the observer, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency, and Δf/f = Δλ/λ, so Δf = 0.0020 × 5.00 × 10¹⁴ = 1.0 × 10¹² Hz and f′ = 5.00 × 10¹⁴ − 0.01 × 10¹⁴ = 4.99 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

questions.stem: Over a cycle lasting 12 days, the absorption lines in the spectrum of a star shift to slightly longer wavelengths, return to their laboratory values, shift to slightly shorter wavelengths, return to their laboratory values, and then repeat the cycle. What can be deduced from these observations?

options.text: The star's distance varies; its lines are longest when it is farthest.
The star's temperature varies, so its light is alternately redder and bluer.
The speed of the star's light alternately increases and decreases.
The star's velocity along our line of sight alternates in direction.

questions.stem: A string of length 0.60 m is fixed at one end. Its other end is free: it is tied to a light ring that slides without friction on a vertical rod. The speed of waves on the string is 240 m s⁻¹. Which gives the harmonic number n, the wavelength λ and the frequency f of the standing wave with the next frequency above that of the first harmonic?

A radio receiver contains a circuit whose natural frequency can be adjusted. Signals from many stations, each broadcasting at a different frequency, reach its aerial at the same time. How does the receiver pick out one station?

options.text: It responds most strongly to the strongest signal, whatever its frequency.
It responds most strongly to the signal with the highest frequency reaching it.
It oscillates at its own natural frequency, whatever signals reach the aerial.
Its natural frequency is set equal to that station's frequency, so it resonates with it.

questions.explanation: This is a useful application of resonance. The circuit responds with a large amplitude only to a signal at (or very near) its natural frequency, so adjusting that frequency to match one station selects it while the others produce only small responses.

questions.stem: A radar speed detector at the roadside emits microwaves of frequency f along a straight road. The microwaves reflected from a car on the road are detected with a frequency slightly lower than f. What can be deduced about the car?

options.text: It is a long way from the detector, whatever its motion.
It is at rest, and the microwaves lost energy on reflection.
It is moving along the road, away from the detector.
Nothing about its motion: no Doppler shift occurs at road speeds.

questions.explanation: A lower frequency means the reflected wavefronts return less often than they were emitted, which happens when the reflector is receding. Radar speed detectors use the size of this shift to find the car's speed.

questions.stem: A pipe of length 0.68 m is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound in the air in the pipe is 340 m s⁻¹. Which gives, in increasing order, the lowest frequencies at which the air in the pipe resonates?

options.text: f = 125 Hz and no other

questions.explanation: A closed end is a displacement node and an open end an antinode, so L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, … The first harmonic has λ = 4 × 0.68 = 2.72 m and f₁ = 340/2.72 = 125 Hz; only odd harmonics exist, giving 125, 375 and 625 Hz.

questions.stem: A pipe is open at both ends. The air in the pipe vibrates in its first harmonic. Which statement about the motion of the air is correct?

options.text: The air at the midpoint of the pipe does not oscillate.
The air at each open end oscillates side to side across the pipe.
The air at each open end of the pipe does not oscillate.
The air oscillates with the same amplitude all along the pipe.

questions.explanation: Each open end is a displacement antinode and, in the first harmonic of a pipe open at both ends (L = λ/2), there is a single displacement node midway along the pipe. At the node the displacement of the air is zero at all times, so the air there does not oscillate.

questions.stem: White light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. Which describes the pattern seen on a screen?

options.text: A white central maximum, with a spectrum in each order on either side and violet nearest the centre
A white central maximum, with a spectrum in each order on either side and red nearest the centre
A spectrum at the centre, as well as in each order on either side, with violet nearest to the centre
A white central maximum and a white maximum in each order, as all colours share the same angles

questions.explanation: At the central maximum (n = 0) the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all colours coincide and it is white. In each higher order sin θ = nλ/d is larger for longer wavelengths, so each spectrum runs from violet (nearest the centre) to red (farthest out).

questions.stem: Light containing just two wavelengths, 450 nm and 700 nm, is incident normally on a diffraction grating with slit spacing d = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Which statement about the maxima produced is correct?

options.text: On each side, the 450 nm light gives maxima up to order 4, and the 700 nm light up to order 3.
On each side, the 450 nm light gives maxima up to order 4, but the 700 nm light only up to order 2.
The 700 nm light gives more orders than the 450 nm light, because red light is deviated less.
Both wavelengths give maxima up to the same order, as the grating alone fixes the maxima.
